items.text: What did Epps v 4 Quarters Restoration (2015) hold about a contract between a homeowner and an unlicensed builder: void or voidable?
Voidable, not void. A voidable contract is valid and enforceable unless and until the homeowner elects to void it. Epps v 4 Quarters Restoration, 498 Mich 518 (2015).
In Epps, was the voidable-contract holding limited to any particular fact pattern?

Yes. The Court expressly limited its voidable-not-void ruling to an innocent homeowner: there was no indication the Epps knew their contractor was unlicensed. The Court did not decide whether a knowing homeowner gets the same treatment.
What does 'shield, not sword' mean in Epps regarding MCL 339.2412(1)?

MCL 339.2412(1) bars an unlicensed contractor from bringing a lawsuit to collect compensation, but it does not bar the contractor from defending itself, and it does not give the homeowner an independent right to sue to claw back money already paid.
Does MCL 339.2412(1)'s bar on suing depend on whether the homeowner knew the contractor was unlicensed?
No. The statute's text only requires the contractor to allege and prove it was licensed during performance. It has no exception for what the homeowner knew or didn't know.
Under MCL 339.2412(3), can an unlicensed contractor place a construction lien on the homeowner's property?
No. An unlicensed person or qualifying officer cannot impose or take legal action to impose a lien on real property for work performed while unlicensed.
What civil fine can a prosecutor or the attorney general obtain under MCL 339.2412(4) against an unlicensed contractor?
A civil fine of not less than $5,000.00 and not more than $25,000.00, apart from any civil damages or restitution.
What must a written contract state under MCL 570.1114 to preserve a contractor's right to a residential construction lien?

That a license is required for the work under Article 24 (or the applicable skilled trade article), and, if the contractor must be licensed, that the contractor is licensed and its license number. There is no dollar-amount floor.
Under MCL 570.1114, does a verbal residential improvement contract preserve lien rights?
No. The contractor has no right to a construction lien on a residential structure unless the improvement was provided under a written contract, with any amendments also in writing.
How many days does a subcontractor or supplier have to serve a Notice of Furnishing under MCL 570.1109(1)?
20 days after furnishing the first labor or material.
Does a general contractor with a direct contract with the homeowner need to serve a Notice of Furnishing?
No. MCL 570.1109(1) says a contractor is not required to provide a notice of furnishing to preserve lien rights arising from a contract directly with the owner or lessee.
Within how many days after last furnishing labor or material must a claim of lien be recorded under MCL 570.1111(1)?
90 days, with the register of deeds in the county where the property is located, or the right to a construction lien ceases to exist.
Within how many days after recording must a construction lien be enforced through foreclosure under MCL 570.1117(1)?
1 year after the date the claim of lien was recorded.
When must a contractor give the homeowner a sworn statement under MCL 570.1110?
When payment is due to the contractor, when the contractor requests payment, or when a demand for the sworn statement has been made by or on behalf of the owner.
What is the operative rule of Roger Williams Ins Co v Carrington (1880) about post-loss assignment of an insurance claim?

An assignment made after the loss did not require the insurer's consent. A policy provision forfeiting coverage for an assignment without consent is invalid as applied to the transfer of an accrued cause of action, because the absolute right to assign such claims cannot be prevented.
What did Jawad A. Shah, M.D., PC v State Farm (2018) hold about an anti-assignment clause and a post-loss claim?

The anti-assignment clause was unenforceable to prohibit an assignment made after the loss of an accrued claim to payment, because enforcing it in that circumstance would violate Michigan public policy under Roger Williams v Carrington.
Is Shah v State Farm a property-insurance case or a no-fault case?

A no-fault case. Healthcare providers took a post-loss assignment of a patient's no-fault benefits claim. The court applies the same common-law post-loss assignment rule from Roger Williams v Carrington that would apply to a property claim.
Does an anti-assignment clause block a post-loss transfer of an already-accrued insurance claim in Michigan?

No. Under Roger Williams v Carrington (1880) and Shah v State Farm (2018), an anti-assignment clause is unenforceable against the assignment of an accrued claim after the loss has occurred, though it remains enforceable against a pre-loss transfer of the policy itself.
Has Michigan enacted a statute specifically regulating post-loss assignment of property-insurance benefits?
No. Michigan has not enacted a property AOB statute. The post-loss assignment rule remains pure common law from Roger Williams v Carrington (1880).
Who does MCL 500.2006(4)'s 12% penalty interest belong to?
The insured or a person directly entitled to benefits under the insured's insurance contract (or, under a different standard, a third-party tort claimant).
Does any published Michigan property-insurance case hold that a contractor-assignee is 'a person directly entitled to benefits' for 12% interest purposes?

No. No published Michigan property case squarely resolves this. The safest framing is that the contractor may pursue the 12% derivatively through the homeowner's assigned right, not as its own independent entitlement.
What does an assignment of benefits give a contractor with respect to a homeowner's insurance claim?
Standing to sue the carrier as an assignee for the assigned, accrued claim, stepping into the homeowner's contractual shoes. It does not create new rights the homeowner did not already have.
Does holding an assignment of benefits let a contractor negotiate or adjust the claim with the carrier for a fee?
No. That would be adjusting a loss for compensation, which requires an adjuster license under MCL 500.1222, regardless of any assignment of benefits.
What does MCL 445.904(1)(a) exempt from the Michigan Consumer Protection Act?
A transaction or conduct specifically authorized under laws administered by a regulatory board or officer acting under statutory authority of Michigan or the United States.
Under current MCL 445.904(3), does the Michigan Consumer Protection Act create a cause of action for chapter 20 insurance-code violations occurring on or after March 28, 2001?

No. The MCPA does not apply to, or create a cause of action for, an unfair, unconscionable, or deceptive practice made unlawful by chapter 20 of the insurance code when it occurred on or after March 28, 2001.
In Smith v Globe Life Ins Co (1999), why did the plaintiff's MCPA claim against the insurer survive at that time?

Because the version of MCL 445.904(2) then in force expressly permitted private actions to be brought under section 11 for chapter-20-type insurance conduct. That carve-out has since been closed by later amendment.
TRAP: Does Smith v Globe Life Ins Co (1999) mean the Michigan Consumer Protection Act never applies to insurers today?

Not quite. Smith actually let an MCPA claim proceed in 1999 under a since-closed statutory carve-out. It is the current MCL 445.904(3), not the 1999 holding by itself, that bars an MCPA cause of action for chapter-20 conduct today.
What is the current small claims division jurisdictional dollar limit in Michigan under MCL 600.8401?
$7,000, effective beginning January 1, 2024.
Can an attorney represent a party in Michigan small claims court under MCL 600.8408(1)?

No, except an attorney appearing on the attorney's own behalf. Attorneys, collection agencies, and anyone other than the plaintiff and defendant are barred from taking part in small claims litigation.
Under MCL 600.8408, can a party remove a case out of small claims to the general civil division?
Yes, before trial begins, upon demand. Once both parties commence a trial in small claims, they waive that removal right.
What is the HIFA rescission deadline under MCL 445.1202(c)(4)?
Not later than 5 p.m. on the business day following the date of the contract, by written notice.
Does HIFA apply to a standard cash-pay or insurance-pay restoration work authorization?

No. HIFA only applies to a home improvement installment contract where the homeowner finances the job on credit through the contractor, with a cash price over $300. It does not apply where there is no installment financing through the contractor.
What is the HSSA rescission deadline under MCL 445.112(1)?
Until midnight of the third business day after the day the buyer signs the agreement.
TRAP: A homeowner calls a restoration contractor themselves after a pipe bursts. Does HSSA's 3-day cancellation right apply?
No, or at least not automatically. HSSA applies to a home solicitation sale, meaning the seller solicited the sale at the buyer's residence. A homeowner-initiated call is not a seller solicitation.
A restoration contractor with a GC-direct contract with the homeowner is unlicensed during the work. The homeowner refuses to pay. Can the contractor sue to collect?

No. MCL 339.2412(1) bars an unlicensed contractor from bringing or maintaining an action to collect compensation unless it alleges and proves it was licensed during performance. The contract is only voidable, not void, but that does not create a right to sue while unlicensed.
A homeowner sues an unlicensed contractor for breach of contract after a botched restoration job. Can the contractor raise defenses on the merits?
Yes. Epps holds MCL 339.2412(1) is a shield, not a sword: it bars the contractor's own suit to collect, but it does not bar the contractor from defending itself against a claim brought against it.
A homeowner who knew her contractor was unlicensed later wants to void the contract and keep the completed work for free. Does Epps clearly resolve this in her favor?
No. Epps expressly limited its voidable-not-void holding to an innocent homeowner; it did not decide what happens when the homeowner knew. This scenario is an open question, not a settled one.
A licensed GC signs a residential water-loss repair contract but the contract never states the contractor's license number. Can the GC record a construction lien if unpaid?

No. MCL 570.1114 conditions residential lien rights on a written contract that states the licensure requirement and the contractor's actual license number. Missing the license number defeats the lien regardless of the contractor's actual licensure.
A drywall subcontractor starts work on a restoration job on June 1 under a sub-contract with the GC. By what date must it serve a Notice of Furnishing to preserve full lien rights?
By June 21, 20 days after furnishing the first labor or material, served on the designee and general contractor.
A restoration GC last furnished labor on a home on March 1 and remains unpaid. By what date must it record a claim of lien to preserve its right to a construction lien?
By May 30, 90 days after last furnishing labor or material, recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property is located.
A contractor recorded a claim of lien on January 15. By what date must it file suit to foreclose the lien?
By January 15 of the following year, 1 year after the date the claim of lien was recorded.

A water-loss homeowner signs an assignment of benefits at intake for mitigation work already completed. The carrier's policy has an anti-assignment clause requiring its consent. Is the assignment enforceable?
Yes. Under Roger Williams v Carrington and Shah v State Farm, an anti-assignment clause is unenforceable against the post-loss assignment of an accrued claim, regardless of the insurer's consent.

Before any loss occurs, a homeowner tries to assign her future insurance policy rights to a contractor as a marketing incentive. Does the post-loss assignment rule from Roger Williams protect this assignment?

No. Roger Williams and Shah protect assignments of an already-accrued claim made after a loss. A pre-loss transfer of the policy itself remains subject to the anti-assignment clause and the insurer's consent.
A contractor holding an AOB sues the carrier for a late-paid claim and asks for the 12% penalty interest under MCL 500.2006(4) in its own name as an independent right. Is this the safest framing?

No. No published Michigan property case gives a contractor-assignee an independent right to the 12% interest. The safer framing is that the contractor enforces the homeowner's derivative right to that interest through the assignment.
A restoration company holding an AOB tells the carrier's adjuster it will 'settle the disputed scope' for a fee equal to 15% of whatever additional amount it recovers. Is this permitted under an AOB?

No. Negotiating or settling a disputed claim for a contingent fee is adjusting a loss for compensation under MCL 500.1222, which requires an adjuster license the contractor does not have, and an AOB does not authorize it.
A homeowner sues her insurer under the Michigan Consumer Protection Act for misrepresenting how it processed her 2026 water-damage claim. Will the MCPA claim survive?

No, most likely not. Under current MCL 445.904(3), the MCPA does not apply to or create a cause of action for chapter-20 insurance-code conduct occurring on or after March 28, 2001, which covers 2026 claims-handling conduct.
A contractor is owed $6,500 by a homeowner for an unpaid balance on a small mitigation job. What Michigan court can it use without hiring a lawyer, and can the homeowner bring one?

Small claims division, since $6,500 is under the $7,000 jurisdictional limit of MCL 600.8401. Neither side may bring an attorney under MCL 600.8408(1), unless a party removes the case to the general civil division before trial.
A contractor is owed $9,000 after an AOB dispute with a carrier. Can it file in small claims?
No. $9,000 exceeds the $7,000 jurisdictional limit of MCL 600.8401. It must use the general civil division instead.

A homeowner signs a financed home-improvement installment contract with a restoration contractor for $2,000 of upgrade work beyond what insurance covers, on a Tuesday. By when can she rescind under HIFA?
By 5 p.m. on Wednesday, the business day following the date of the contract, by written notice under MCL 445.1202(c)(4).
A door-to-door storm-damage solicitor signs a homeowner up for a full roof replacement on her porch on a Monday. By when can she cancel under HSSA, absent a valid emergency waiver?
Until midnight of the Thursday following, the third business day after she signed, under MCL 445.112(1).
A mitigation company wants to start water extraction the same day it is solicited at the home, before the HSSA 3-day window runs. What exactly must the homeowner sign to waive that right?

A separate, dated, signed personal statement written in the homeowner's own handwriting describing the emergency and expressly waiving the 3-business-day right to cancel, in addition to the company substantially beginning performance in good faith.
A mitigation company has the homeowner sign a pre-printed emergency waiver paragraph at the bottom of its standard work order. Does this satisfy the HSSA emergency exception?
No. MCL 445.112(5)(b) requires a separate, dated, signed statement in the buyer's own handwriting, not a pre-printed or typed clause on the standard contract.

A restoration company that also employs a licensed adjuster wants that adjuster to also serve as the company's estimator and negotiate the same homeowner's claim with the carrier for a contingent fee. Is this safe under Michigan law?

No. This is the conflict that ended Aleksandr Guldshtadt's adjuster license: DIFS revoked it and fined him $50,000 on April 1, 2026 for holding a financial interest in a fire repair contractor, using unapproved adjusting contracts, and diverting claim money to his contracting business. MCL 500.1224(4) also bars issuing an adjuster license to anyone connected with a fire repair contractor, and negotiating the claim for a fee tied to the payout is unlicensed adjusting under MCL 500.1222.

A homeowner repairs her own fire-damaged house instead of hiring a general contractor, and the carrier deducts 20% for contractor overhead and profit from the actual cash value payment. Does the fact that she self-performed settle whether O&P is owed?

No. In Salesin v State Farm the insured repaired his own home, and the court held that his not actually incurring overhead and profit was 'not dispositive.' The test adopted from Gilderman is whether the insured was reasonably likely to incur the cost, so there is no automatic rule either way. Domain 02 covers this in depth.

A contractor signed a residential lien-eligible written contract with the correct license number, completed the work, and the homeowner requests a sworn statement before final payment. What must the contractor provide, and what happens if it lies?
A sworn statement listing every sub, supplier, and unpaid laborer with amounts due. A false sworn statement given with intent to defraud is a crime under MCL 570.1110.

Worked example: a water-loss homeowner signs an AOB and work authorization at intake with the license number included. The carrier underpays reconstruction by $9,000 and disputes scope. What is one thing the contractor can legitimately do?

Rely on the AOB to communicate directly with the carrier about the assigned, already-incurred charges, and if unpaid, record a claim of lien within 90 days of last furnishing labor or material under MCL 570.1111, since the written-contract and license-number conditions of MCL 570.1114 were met.

Worked example continued: the same contractor wants to personally negotiate down the $9,000 scope dispute with the adjuster in exchange for a percentage of whatever extra it recovers. Is this within the contractor's rights under the AOB?

No. Negotiating a disputed claim for a contingent fee is unlicensed adjusting under MCL 500.1222, and the 10% fee cap and licensing bar in MCL 500.1226 and 500.1224 exist precisely to prevent this, regardless of the AOB.
TRAP: Is the 20-day Notice of Furnishing clock in MCL 570.1109 the same for a laborer as for a subcontractor or supplier?

No. MCL 570.1109(1) gives a subcontractor or supplier 20 days after furnishing the first labor or material. MCL 570.1109(2) gives a laborer 30 days after wages were contractually due but were not paid. A contractor in direct contract with the owner serves no notice at all.
